items.title: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast, cost-effective, and reliable video generation and editing now generally available
items.summary:
Today, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is generally available on Google Cloud. Built for the everyday videos businesses make in volume — like product videos, virtual try-ons, and ads — this model is fast, cost-effective, and follows your image, video and audio references more closely than before.  

Business users can create with it in Gemini for business and Google Vids, and developers can build with it via API.

Here's what's new:

  • A lower price: $0.07 per second of 720p video, 30% less than Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash, with similar savings at other resolutions.
  • Longer clips: Generate and edit videos of up to 15 seconds, up from 10s.
  • More consistent results: stronger adherence to image and video references keeps products, characters, and brand details consistent from shot to shot.
  • Faster drafts, in higher resolution: create drafts at 360p or 720p, then upscale the best creations to 1080p or 4K.
  • More natural speech: You can generate scenes with more fluid, natural-sounding dialogue, clearer lip-sync, and distinct multi-speaker conditioning.
  • Editing in conversation: refine the same clip, such as swapping a product, changing lighting, or changing camera angle, instead of starting over.

Note: Audio references are gated behind allowlisting.

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is ready for production

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is production-ready and backed by Google Cloud’s enterprise-grade infrastructure and security, offering Provisioned Throughput. Outputs carry an imperceptible SynthID watermark.

Video creation inside the tools people already use

Design and creative platforms are building Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash directly into their products, so their users can create and edit videos where they already work. Here’s how customers are already using Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash:

“At Artlist, we’re focused on giving creators the control and flexibility to bring their ideas to life. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash brings exciting capabilities in reference-based generation, video extension, and creative consistency, helping our customers move from experimentation to professional content production at scale.” – Roee Peled, CPTO, Artlist.

Artlist uses Gemini 1.2 Omni Flash to bring creative ideas to life

“Creative teams need models that they can rely on consistently. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash edits exactly what you ask for, a colorway or a background, and leaves the product untouched, even from detailed images and finished video. Its video-to-video takes footage into entirely new styles.” – Andrew Taco Zhang, Product Marketing Manager, FLORA.

FLORA uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to create new styles

“We ran Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash through our evals at invideo. Honestly, it's really good. It sticks to the prompt, and the physics and sound feel real. If you need fast video at scale, it's one of the best we've tested. And 15 seconds means a full scene in one go.” – Shivam Rastogi, VP of Engineering, invideo.

invideo uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to create full scenes in one prompt

“We’re really impressed by how fast and accurate this new model is. The outputs retain an amazing level of detail, and the model does a great job of making only the changes we ask for while keeping everything else consistent. We’re excited to use it for character and scene replacements, as well as other creative workflows.” – Numan Khan, Creative Specialist, Krea.

Krea uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash for their creative workflows, from character to scene replacements

"Gemini Omni 1.2 fits the way our teams work. Draft mode lets us iterate concepts in minutes, then render in 4K for TV-ready AI dramas. Text stays crisp across frames, characters look and sound real, and the speed keeps production moving. Now that it is generally available, we can bring this quality to over 100M Picsart creators." – Narek Hayrapetyan, Head of Product and Partnerships, Picsart.

Picsart uses Gemini 1.2 Flash to iterate concepts in minutes

Runway empowers creatives with advanced AI video tools to produce high-quality content. For organizations, Runway’s enterprise solutions deliver robust collaborative tools to scale professional production. Here is what they created with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash.

Runway uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to produce and scale high-quality content

Product and listing videos at catalog scale

Retailers and marketplaces use Gemini Omni to turn the photos they already have into short product spins, lifestyle clips, try-on videos, and video ads.

“Photoroom turns product photos into video ads that sell in minutes. We chose Gemini Omni Flash to power our Video Ad Maker and Product Animator because it balances quality, speed and cost. Version 1.2 brings 15-second videos, a top user request. With general availability and SLAs, we can rely on it in production for our sellers and enterprise customers.” - Matt Rouif, CEO and Co-founder, Photoroom.

Photoroom uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to power their Video Ad Maker and Product Animator

“QuickFrame AI helps marketers and business owners create, edit, and launch professional-quality ads for CTV and social in minutes. With Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash now supporting 15-second video generations at 1080p, users can create a complete CTV ad in a single generation, making TV ad creation simpler for businesses of all sizes.” - Richard Girges, Chief Technology Officer, QuickFrame AI.

QuickFrame AI uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to create complete CTV ads in a single generation

Create in Gemini for business, Google Vids and build with the API

Coming soon to Gemini, business users will be able to create a short video from a prompt or a product photo, right in the chat. In Google Vids, teams can combine generated clips with avatars, music and voiceover to create product explainers, teasers, social posts and sales pitches. Businesses can also embed the capabilities of Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash into their applications and agents via the API.

Get started with Gemini Omni

We'll keep improving Gemini Omni based on your feedback, so tell us what you build.

  • For business users: Try it in Google Vids; coming soon to Gemini for business

  • For developers: Try it in the Google Cloud console, build with the API, and see the pricing

items.title: Balancing hierarchical representation and quantization: A performance trade-off in text embeddings
items.summary: Hierarchical text embedding models offer variable-length representations, while quantization reduces numerical precision; both aim to improve computational efficiency. This work is an empirical benchmark study of how these two orthogonal, already-established techniques interact. We evaluate 38 tasks from the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) using four transformer-based embedding models, covering 1D and 2D hierarchical representations combined with 32-bit, 8-bit, and binary quantization, for 168 configurations per task. We report each efficiency dimension separately: theoretical per-vector storage and end-to-end evaluation time. Under a Friedman test with Nemenyi post-hoc analysis, int8 quantization is statistically indistinguishable from float32 for pair classification and re-ranking and costs at most 1.5 percentage points overall, whereas binary quantization is significantly worse across every task category. Halving the embedding dimension once is not statistically detectable above $m=16$; two successive halvings always are. Combining an 8x dimensionality reduction with int8 yields a 32x reduction in per-vector storage at 94.4% of baseline effectiveness. Because evaluation times were measured once, we treat them as indicative: we find no evidence that quantization speeds up evaluation, whereas sampling from intermediate layers shortens it substantially. Retrieval degrades far faster than every other category, so we report findings per task category.

items.title: ArcRAG: Agentic Compositional Retrieval over Knowledge Graphs
items.summary: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) answers questions by retrieving over a knowledge graph built from a corpus. Yet retrieval strategies are designed around the structure their own construction pipeline produces, and whether they survive a change of construction is rarely tested. We study this cross-construction portability: whether one retrieval procedure, with no construction-specific schema, relation names, or retuning, stays effective when the graph is built differently. We introduce ArcRAG, which induces a query-local graph interface at inference time (the node labels, relation descriptors, and property keys reachable from the entities a question names), plans multi-hop traversals against it, and executes and repairs them as Cypher. We build each of the MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and TriviaQA corpora as a schema-guided graph (typed nodes, a closed relation set, source provenance) and as an open-information-extraction graph (untyped nodes, free-text relations), with the retriever's configuration fixed across them. We compare against a construction-agnostic Direct-Cypher agent, ablate each stage across retry and pass budgets on both graph families, and compare with results reported for prior GraphRAG systems, most of which design retrieval together with their own graph construction. Across the two constructions, we find that retrieval need not be co-designed with the graph: query-time interface induction keeps a construction-agnostic retriever effective when the construction changes, although construction still shapes absolute accuracy.

items.title: LifeVal: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Personalized Agentic Consumer Tasks
items.summary: We introduce LifeVal, a benchmark evaluating AI model performance on personalized agentic consumer tasks. LifeVal covers the most valuable life tasks that a personalized digital superassistant could automate, representing over 1.7 trillion US dollars in annual willingness-to-pay across 148 consumer task categories (e.g., managing finances, moving apartments, searching for a job, finding childcare). To construct our activity distribution, we conducted a new survey of willingness-to-pay for a digital superassistant across a demographically representative sample of over 3,800 consumers, cross-referencing our results against the American Time Use Survey (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025) and the Multinational Time Use Study (Fisher et al., 2025). For the most valuable consumer activities, we recruited task creators to create AI evaluation tasks personalized using real ChatGPT conversations and memories, reference files, and personal context. Task creators had to pass our expertise threshold (including personally completing the task multiple times and seeing the results through in their real lives for over a year) and also write a rubric, ensuring that our evaluation measured the best personalized completion for that task. All tasks had to pass at least three rounds of human quality-control before acceptance into our final evaluation sets.

items.story_key: story|title:from delta sharing to opensharing what changed what s next
items.content_excerpt: How Delta Sharing became OpenSharing, an open, vendor-neutral protocol that extends zero-copy sharing beyond tables to agent skills, AI models, and unstructured data across platforms, and what the change means if you already share data today. Delta Sharing has been the way thousands of organizations exchange live data across clouds and platforms without copying it. In June 2026, Databricks and the Linux Foundation announced that Delta Sharing has evolved into OpenSharing , an open, vendor-neutral protocol for sharing not just tables, but the broader set of assets that AI teams now depend on: agent skills, AI models, and unstructured data. If you already share data with Delta Sharing, or you're evaluating how to collaborate with partners on both data and AI assets, this post walks through what OpenSharing actually is, what's changed under the hood, and where the project is headed. When Databricks introduced Delta Sharing at Data + AI Summit 2021, the core problem it addressed was simple to state and hard to solve well: organizations wanted to share live data with partners, customers, and other teams, without exporting files, standing up brittle ETL jobs, or forcing every recipient onto the same platform. Delta Sharing was contributed to the Linux Foundation as an open protocol, built on Delta Lake and Parquet, so a provider could grant access to a table and a recipient could query it directly, in real time, from tools like Apache Spark, Power BI, Tableau, pandas, and many others. That open, zero-copy model resonated. Delta Sharing grew into the most widely adopted open protocol for secure data sharing, used by organizations including Amadeus, Atlassian, LSEG, SAP, Stripe, and The Trade Desk for cross-cloud and cross-platform collaboration, according to Databricks ( Databricks press release ). By the time Databricks announced OpenSharing in June 2026, Delta Sharing had reached more than 28,000 data recipients, with roughly a third of shares flowing across platforms through open connectors rather than staying inside Databricks-to-Databricks sharing ( Databricks blog ). Sharing had already grown well beyond tables. Through Databricks-to-Databricks sharing, teams were exchanging views, volumes of unstructured files, notebooks, and registered ML models years before agents entered the picture, so structured data was never the whole story. items.title: More Performance From Every Byte: How Full-Stack Codesign Solves AI’s Memory Challenge
items.summary: Larger models, longer contexts and agentic applications are increasing GPU memory pressure while supply tightens and prices rise — a trend expected to continue through the near term. NVIDIA works closely with memory partners to rapidly adopt the latest memory technologies. NVIDIA was first to adopt HBM3e and HBM4 technologies into an accelerated computing stack.  […]
items.story_key: story|title:more performance from every byte how full stack codesign solves ai s memory chal
items.content_excerpt: Larger models, longer contexts and agentic applications are increasing GPU memory pressure while supply tightens and prices rise — a trend expected to continue through the near term. NVIDIA works closely with memory partners to rapidly adopt the latest memory technologies. NVIDIA was first to adopt HBM3e and HBM4 technologies into an accelerated computing stack. But the approach isn’t to simply pack more memory onto the GPU. It’s full-stack codesign. NVIDIA intentionally designs GPUs, CPUs, networking, storage and software together to get more useful work out of memory at every layer of the AI factory. That matters because an AI factory runs on a memory and storage hierarchy. GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is the fastest, most expensive and most contested tier — with model weights and KV cache competing for limited capacity. Below it sit CPU memory, local SSDs and shared storage, each trading speed for more capacity at a lower cost per bit. How much useful work a byte does depends on how well the whole hierarchy is used: shrinking what must be stored, placing it on the right tier and bringing it back to the GPU before it’s needed. Byte for byte, NVIDIA makes the most efficient use of memory at every layer — and the results show it. From NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra to the Vera Rubin platform, HBM capacity per GPU rose roughly 3%, while agentic throughput per dollar rose by up to 30x on SemiAnalysis AgentX. Frontier models now have trillions of parameters — the values that hold what an AI model learned in training. KV cache, which holds the context the model needs to understand each active request without reprocessing the same information, is also expanding. Agentic trajectories carry prior context across repeated model and tool calls, in some cases processing up to 3 million tokens, so each request’s working memory grows over time. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) adds relevant enterprise information to prompts, creating even more context to process and retain. During inference, HBM primarily holds both model parameters and KV cache. The result: greater pressure on HBM. Adding more HBM capacity per GPU is the obvious response to that pressure, but capacity delivers only what bandwidth can move. Think of HBM as a warehouse and memory bandwidth as its loading docks. items.title: How big is the open model economy today?
items.summary: Our first open model economy research note for paid subscribers.
items.story_key: story|title:how big is the open model economy today
items.content_excerpt: My longest running agent testbed has been building the Interconnects Dashboard — an aggregator of all of the best data on open model adoption and performance from across the web. This dashboard is freely available and becoming quite useful. Still, all the measurements we have on open model adoption are incredibly imprecise. We have noisy platform metrics, marketing-related metrics from startups, and imperfect public evaluations. It takes an informed eye to figure out where things are going. These research notes are my current best approximations of where we stand. As with most things on Interconnects, our goal is to build well more value than we capture, so the data on the dashboard will remain free for the foreseeable future. These notes will be more raw than many of my articles, a place for sharing what I’m mulling over but don’t have complete evidence for (yet). They will be primarily paid, enabling me to speak more freely. If you work in AI policy or policy-facing research, please reach out to us and we can likely get discounted or free access. The primary question I wanted to address today is: What is the market for open model inference? Is it growing? Is it a rounding error relative to OpenAI/Anthropic? I’ve been building the best measurements I can here, primarily using the open model inference startups Baseten, Fireworks, and Together AI as the bellwethers here (along with the open model share of OpenRouter’s token volume, which they thankfully report in their API). The hyperscalers also likely have a major footprint here, e.g. Amazon Bedrock and Azure’s model garden, but I haven’t seen them break down usage by model category. The startups’ fates are much more directly correlated with the success of open model inference as a category. For the latest data, we can start with a slide from my talk on the open model economy (recording here ). These are the public disclosures from the open model startups on their token volume, over time, log-scale. This shows near-exponential growth, before the uptick that would follow GLM 5.2’s step change in open agents . For example, Fireworks announced at their first company conference this week that they’re serving more than 40T tokens per day to customers’ customized models. This is just one slice of their inference, a vertical that they said grew over 2x from this summer, so I would expect their total number this fall to be well above 100T tokens when we get the next update. Nimisha Asthagiri shares how applying proven product engineering and architecture principles creates a bounded canvas for AI agents. She explains how this model provides agents with bounded autonomy, continuous drift detection, and decision records to scale software development resiliently.

By Nimisha Asthagiri

Lily Mara explains how to avoid high-risk software rewrites through incremental FFI refactoring. She shares how engineering teams can replace Python bottlenecks with Rust via PyO3, demonstrating how to achieve dramatic function-level speedups, seamless integration testing, and meaningful infrastructure cost savings without microservice overhead. The panelists explain how AI tools and vibe coding reshape frontend and mobile engineering. Advait Patel shares a playbook for securing AI agent systems in production. He discusses moving defense boundaries from the prompt to the tool layer, enforcing scoped workload identities, and mitigating prompt injection via tool outputs. items.title: Maggie Appleton: Agentic Coding Has Outgrown the Text Box
items.summary:
Agentic coding has outgrown the text box. Maggie Appleton, staff research engineer at GitHub Next, argues that walls of CLI output and AGENTS.md files serve coding agents far better than the humans steering them. She walks through Chopin, the GitHub Next prototype where background agents turn a team's planning chat into a structured plan, and makes the case for agents that prompt you instead of waiting to be prompted.

What we cover:
– Why text-heavy agentic coding tools favor agents over humans
– Boundary objects: what AGENTS.md, skill files and MCP servers get right and wrong
– Multiplayer planning with coding agents in GitHub Next's Chopin
– Human-to-agent handoffs, formal verification and spec-driven development
– Why software quality is rising, not falling, with coding agents
– Which roles still matter: PMs, designers and engineers

items.title: Reasoning over Non-Parametric Memory in Multilingual LLMs: A Cognitive-Based Analysis of Relational Knowledge
items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assumes that language models can reason over relations stated in their context rather than fall back on associations memorized during pretraining. We study this evidence-conditioned relational reasoning in isolation, with the facts supplied directly in the prompt rather than retrieved. \textsc{Rel-Bloom} is a controlled multilingual diagnostic of 450 multiple-choice questions built from 30 Wikidata relations; the same source relations are instantiated at five Bloom-inspired levels (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate) and under three veracity conditions (Factual, Counterfactual, Neutralized). Across 43 models, six languages, and two multilingual settings (226,800 predictions), three findings stand out. First, accuracy drops sharply from Apply to Analyze in every evaluated open-weight model series, reaching 47.2 percentage points for the Large Granite bucket, but not for either Gemini model. Second, Evaluate items remain a bottleneck even for models near ceiling on the other task types: Gemini~3.1 Pro averages 99.5\% on the other four levels but 60.7\% on Evaluate. Third, item- and relation-level difficulty rankings are consistently preserved across languages, indicating a difficulty structure partly shared across languages within this benchmark. Across knowledge conditions, Counterfactual contexts are generally harder than Factual ones, while removing entity identities can improve higher-level performance in some model regimes. Greater model capability therefore does not by itself ensure reliable reasoning over supplied relational evidence. Relevant resources are available at: https://huggingface.co/spaces/QCRI/non-parametric-memory-relational-reasoning.

items.title: Where Search Agents Go Off the Rails: Graph-Grounded Step-Level Verification
items.summary: Search-augmented reasoning systems can reach correct answers while making errors in intermediate steps. Reliable auditing must check whether evidence $D$ covers the question $Q$, reasoning $T$ addresses $Q$, and $T$ is grounded in $D$. We introduce GraphRail, which represents requirements, evidence, and reasoning as structured claims and compares them without a generative judge or gold answer. Across three multi-hop QA benchmarks and three reasoning frameworks, GraphRail improves error recall over generative verifiers while remaining stable under stochastic extraction. Its diagnoses can also guide online reasoning, providing a traceable way to detect and correct intermediate errors.

items.summary: Legora can’t read a single trace of what its agent does for a lawyer. The data belongs to the law firm’s clients. How do you build and test an agent when you can’t see its work? Jacob Lauritzen is the CTO of Legora, one of the fastest-growing companies...

Legora can’t read a single trace of what its agent does for a lawyer. The data belongs to the law firm’s clients. How do you build and test an agent when you can’t see its work? Jacob Lauritzen is the CTO of Legora, one of the fastest-growing companies... Legora can’t read a single trace of what its agent does for a lawyer. The data belongs to the law firm’s clients. How do you build and test an agent when you can’t see its work? Jacob Lauritzen is the CTO of Legora, one of the fastest-growing companies in legal tech history. The team started in a Stockholm basement with ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Today, a lawyer can use Legora to draft and edit Word documents, review 10,000 contracts in a single table, or run due diligence. The agent also coordinates work between lawyers, clients, and other agents. When Legora made its own acquisitions, the team used it for diligence. • Why Legora resisted adding a model picker for years, and why it finally added one • Jacob’s estimate that models already do about 60% of legal work well, and why the rest takes a smarter model • How three engineers and three lawyers build test environments modeled on customers’ work, much like the “worlds” used in reinforcement learning • A citation problem where the model got it right 70% of the time, then 99% after one release. Legora didn’t have to change anything. • Tabular Review, the million-cell spreadsheet the industry copied down to the name • How intake works, how agents create lists, and how a list can start another agent • What legal engineers and forward-deployed engineers each do, and who gets to write code • The 300 Spartans slide Jacob used to argue that 20 engineers would be enough forever. Now there are 100, and he still feels short-handed. • Why Jacob finds Fable and Opus too chatty for drafting and likes Astra’s concise writing • What happens to law firm partnerships, the billable hour, and jobs for junior lawyers 11:03 When evals didn’t seem worth it and one release took citations from 70% to 99% Latent Space is read by the people shipping agents, models and infrastructure. items.title: vLLM Delivers Day-0 Support for Kimi K3.1 Pro
items.summary: vLLM supports Kimi K3.1 Pro on day 0: sparse attention on a KDA hybrid, a packed KV cache with FP8 or NVFP4 latents and MXFP4 index keys, token-sharded prefill, decode context parallelism, and fused low-latency decode.
items.story_key: model:vllm|ver:3.1|variant:pro|title:vllm delivers day 0 support for kimi k3 1 pro
items.content_excerpt: Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot AI's most capable open-weight model: a 2.8T-parameter (104B active) multimodal MoE with a 1M-token context that matches the strongest closed-source models on coding, agentic and knowledge benchmarks. The main change is attention: K3.1 Pro adds Sparse Attention (DSA) to all 24 full-attention layers for efficiency. vLLM supports it on day 0 on NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, Google TPUs and Alibaba T-Head Zhenwu PPUs. Each sparse attention layer has a small indexer next to its MLA attention. The indexer keeps one FP8 key per token (132 bytes with its scale) and scores every earlier token for each query with 32 lightweight heads. Then it keeps the top 2,048 tokens. MLA attention then runs exactly, but only over those 2,048 tokens. DSA was introduced in DeepSeek-V3.2; our DeepSeek-V3.2 post covers the indexer in more detail. The payoff is largest in long-context decode, which is bound by memory bandwidth. Dense MLA reads 576 bytes of FP8 latent per context token per layer. DSA still scans the whole context, but only the 132-byte index keys. It then reads the full latent for just 2,048 tokens. At long context, that is about 23% of the bytes dense MLA reads per layer. Figure 1: Sparse attention (DSA) in Kimi K3.1 Pro. The indexer scores every past token, keeps the top 2,048, and every query head attends exactly over only those tokens' latents. Step through it. The index keys are a second per-token cache next to the MLA latent. Under tensor parallelism (TP) both are replicated on every GPU; KDA state is per request, as in K3. The latent and the index keys can be quantized independently. An NVFP4 latent alone already brings K3.1 Pro below K3 with FP8. Opt-in MXFP4 index keys fit 11% more tokens on top and make the indexer 10–20% faster at long context. With both, eight GB300 GPUs hold 1.7× as many tokens as with FP8, and DCP8 multiplies that by seven: about 36 full 1M-token contexts at once, against 3 for TP8 with FP8. Figure 2: Measured KV cache capacity on 8× GB300. Change the latent and index-key formats, the parallelism, or the context length to see how many full contexts fit. Each DSA layer stores two per-token caches of different widths: the MLA latent (576 bytes in FP8, 352 in NVFP4) and the index keys (132 bytes in FP8, 68 in MXFP4). Neither width is a multiple of the other. The 69 KDA layers each add a recurrent state per request that is much larger than one layer's page of tokens. items.title: claude-agent-sdk-python v0.2.177
items.summary:
New Features

  • on_failure option for HookMatcher: Control what happens when a hook callback fails. Set on_failure="block" to block the action when a callback raises, returns None, or returns a value the CLI rejects. Defaults to "continue" (treat failure as no decision). Requires a CLI version that supports this option; connecting to an older CLI with on_failure="block" raises CLIConnectionError (#1460)

Internal/Other Changes

  • Updated bundled Claude CLI to version 2.1.317
  • Tests: e2e tests now accept either Bash or PowerShell tool in shell-dependent tests, fixing intermittent failures on Windows (#1467)

PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/claude-agent-sdk/0.2.177/

pip install claude-agent-sdk==0.2.177

items.title: claude-code v2.1.316
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ULTRATHINK, which turns the ultrathink keyword off
  • Added pooled group budgets to the Claude apps gateway: one monthly budget that a group's members share, on top of each member's own limit, set with pooled_budget on the spend limits admin API
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_LOOPED_CROSS_CERT_DROP to keep system cross-certificates that certify each other in a loop, for servers whose private CA needs one
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_EFFORT to set the effort level subagents run at when nothing else names one, instead of inheriting the session's
  • Added managed.policy_mode: layered to the Claude apps gateway: every policy that matches a developer applies, each merged over the ones listed below it, not only the first
  • Added guardrail.input_tagging on Claude apps gateway Bedrock upstreams, which wraps prompts in the input tags that an Amazon Bedrock guardrail's prompt attacks filter needs; all_messages_and_system also tags the system prompt
  • Deprecated fast mode for Opus 4.8 as of October 30, 2026; it will be removed on November 30, 2026. After removal, fast mode requests on Opus 4.8 return an error and do not fall back to standard Opus 4.8. Migrate to Opus 5.5 to keep the speedup
  • Fixed shell commands being left running on macOS and Linux when Claude Code exits by itself, for example when credentials are refused or a cloud session is archived
  • Fixed bash aliases with line breaks in their value (except in Git Bash), and functions whose names start with a dash, being garbled or lost in the Bash tool's shell
  • Fixed bash scripts started from the Bash tool stopping after their first command when SHELLOPTS is exported
  • Fixed PowerShell hooks not blocking on exit code 2 when the command begins with a type cast, param, using or an attribute
  • Fixed some network requests hanging when a compressed response was cut off or corrupted
  • Fixed sonnet, opus and haiku on Vertex AI and Amazon Bedrock showing an error mid-session instead of switching to an older model when the newest is not yet available to the account or region
  • Fixed the Claude apps gateway not checking every model a request names against availableModels, deniedModels and models; a request that names a blocked model now gets a 400 naming the field
  • Fixed claude auth login refusing to run where managed settings require a Claude apps gateway; in a terminal it now shows the gateway sign-in
  • Fixed --restricted sessions uploading files from outside the working directories when a Read allow rule covered them
  • Fixed prompts containing invisible characters needing a second Enter to send; plain prompts now send cleaned on the first Enter, and commands still wait for review
  • Fixed sub-agents that inherited a parent sub-agent's model moving to the main model when a background job or message woke them
  • Fixed a managed autoMode.allow list without "$defaults" getting the built-in exceptions back from a host app's --settings, a first rule added in /permissions, or /auto-mode-setup
  • Fixed cloud sessions and cloud scheduled tasks not being marked as failed when auto mode stopped a turn because the server returned no safety verdict
  • Fixed claude -p text output sometimes not saying why auto mode stopped a turn when a background agent was still running
  • Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=1 being ignored in sessions started by a host application (such as Claude Desktop) behind a proxy or LLM gateway with experimental betas turned off
  • Fixed plugin MCP headersHelper scripts receiving a corrupted CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT and server URL when a credential-named environment variable was set to a switch value such as 1
  • Fixed the SDK register_repo_root control request not loading the CLAUDE.md of a directory outside the working directory (with CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD=1)
  • Fixed the Artifact tool showing ? for artifact database access rules at the self level, and not quoting those rules back when it refuses a republish that would drop them
  • Fixed /model <id> not warning when the model isn't recognized by this version and auto-compact will assume a 200K context window
  • Fixed the "hold space to speak" hint using up its three showings in one session, and showing an empty key when push-to-talk is unbound
  • Fixed Grep and Glob never returning when the search process is killed at the timeout but does not exit, seen on Windows
  • Fixed a rare case where resuming a conversation did not restore its plan, when /clear or /resume had been run while part of that conversation was still being saved
  • Fixed first-run setup dropping words from the security notes and the terminal-setup explanation in narrow terminals
  • Fixed the Enterprise survey card taking a typed 1 or 0 after a short pause; a typed answer now needs Enter
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a message sent while Claude was working being answered after a Stop, once the session's process had been replaced
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed an MCP server's on/off switch sometimes being lost when a session moved to a new machine
  • Windows: Fixed the Bash tool losing your aliases and functions in Git Bash when the rc file sets errexit and pipefail and only winpty aliases, or none, are defined
  • Improved /code-review started from the Code tab in Claude Desktop or on the web: cloud and claude remote-control sessions now show the findings card, not a plain-text list
  • Improved /diff on large repositories: each refresh usually runs one fewer full-repository git command, and refreshes are spaced out when git is slow
  • Improved the messages shown when /ultrareview, a cloud session or a cloud agent finds no GitHub remote: they now say to create a repository at https://github.com/new, and /ultrareview no longer suggests a gh command that gh rejects
  • Improved SSL certificate errors to name the likely causes, among them a server that leaves out an intermediate certificate, and the fix for each
  • Changed auto mode so that an autoMode.allow list without "$defaults" no longer removes the built-in rule on scheduled-task prompts
  • Changed server-managed settings for Team and Enterprise logins: settings fetched from Anthropic's API now apply without an approval prompt, and a stored copy that doesn't verify is refused
  • [VSCode] Added sign-in to a Claude apps gateway from the chat panel, with no terminal needed
  • [VSCode] Changed ultrathink to run its turn at xhigh effort and show in a rainbow in the chat box, as in the terminal
  • [VSCode] Fixed the missing Effort slider, Ultracode switch and model name when the model setting has the [1m] tag, such as opus[1m]
  • [VSCode] Fixed saved /btw side-question history being deleted too early while a settings file has errors
  • [VSCode] Fixed a conversation coming back in Auto mode after a reload or restart when its plan was approved with "Yes, and manually approve edits"
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a form card to cloud sessions, so you can fill in or decline a form an MCP server asks for instead of the request being canceled without you seeing it
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a "Catching up…" line that shows while a cloud or Remote Control session you switch back to is still bringing its messages up to date
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed network secrets so Enterprise members can add and delete them on their own cloud environments, instead of only viewing them
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the Changes pane for cloud sessions: the note about what the list leaves out is now a badge beside the branch name, not a row above the diff
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed file search in a cloud session's Files pane showing folders as ../.. paths after Claude changed directory; results now show their path from the project's root
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude refusing to edit or append to a canvas it made in a Slack channel, from that channel, once the canvas was also shared to another channel or a DM
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed untagged replies going unanswered in a Slack Connect thread when both organizations have installed Claude and Slack delivered the reply to the other organization's app
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed a cloud scheduled task's live status checklist in Slack staying half-done; a run can now edit the top-level messages it posted during that run
  • [Claude Tag] Changed a Slack channel's Respond automatically switch to a "How Claude participates" choice on the channel's Configure page and in Claude Tag admin settings
  • [Code Review] Added a findings-by-severity card to the Code Review analytics page, showing the period's total findings, a daily chart stacked by severity, and each severity's count
